Found it. Your useEffect has no dependency array at all.

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  // this runs after EVERY render
});
```

No second argument means it fires on every render. Each fire calls setUser and setLoading, which trigger a re-render, which fires the effect again. Infinite loop.

Fix:

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`)
    .then(res => res.json())
    .then(data => {
      setUser(data);
      setLoading(false);
    });
}, [userId]);
```

The `[userId]` dependency array means: run this effect once on mount, and again only if userId changes. That's what you want -- fetch when the user changes, not on every render.

Secondary issue: you have no error handling on that fetch. If the API returns 404, `user` stays null and `user.name` throws. Consider adding a `.catch()` with an error state.
That fixed it. The dependency array thing always confuses me. Why does React even allow useEffect without one? It seems like a footgun.

It is a footgun. Dan Abramov has acknowledged this. The reason it exists: sometimes you genuinely want to run an effect after every render. Logging, measuring DOM dimensions after layout changes, synchronizing with an external system on every update. Those are real use cases.

But the API shape -- where omitting an argument is the most dangerous option -- violates the principle of least surprise. A safer design would require you to explicitly write `useEffect(fn, 'every')` for the run-always case. The React team chose consistency (all three behaviors use the same function) over safety (making the dangerous case require explicit opt-in).

That's a design tradeoff, not a mistake. But it's a tradeoff that puts the cost on new developers, which is worth noticing.

CRISPR is a system that lets you edit DNA at a specific location, the way find-and-replace works in a text document. Here's the mechanism at the level you're asking for:

Bacteria evolved CRISPR as an immune system. When a virus attacks, the bacterium stores a snippet of the virus's DNA in its own genome -- a molecular mugshot. Next time that virus appears, the bacterium makes an RNA copy of the mugshot, attaches it to a protein called Cas9, and the RNA guides Cas9 to the matching sequence in the virus's DNA. Cas9 cuts both strands. Virus neutralized.

Scientists realized they could reprogram the guide RNA to target any DNA sequence, not just viruses. Synthesize a guide RNA matching the gene you want to edit, attach it to Cas9, deliver it to a cell. Cas9 finds the matching sequence and cuts. The cell's own repair machinery then either disables the gene (if you just want to knock it out) or inserts a new sequence you provide (if you want to replace it).

The precision is the breakthrough. Previous gene editing was like editing a book by ripping out pages. CRISPR is like editing specific words.

Three catches, in order of difficulty:

**Delivery.** Getting CRISPR into the right cells in a living person is hard. In a petri dish, it's straightforward. In a body with trillions of cells, you need the editing machinery to reach the specific tissue -- liver, lungs, blood, brain -- without editing things you didn't intend. Delivery vehicles (usually modified viruses) are improving but remain the bottleneck.

**Off-target edits.** The guide RNA sometimes matches sequences that are similar but not identical to the target. Cas9 cuts there too. In a lab dish, you can screen for this. In a patient, an off-target cut in the wrong gene could cause cancer or other problems. Newer Cas variants (Cas12, base editors, prime editors) are more precise, but the risk isn't zero.

**Complexity of disease.** Most diseases people want CRISPR to fix aren't caused by a single gene. Sickle cell disease is -- one mutation in one gene -- and CRISPR therapy for it was approved in 2023. That's the proof of concept. But heart disease, diabetes, most cancers, Alzheimer's -- these involve dozens or hundreds of genes interacting with environment. You can't find-and-replace your way out of polygenic disease.

The trajectory is real. CRISPR will transform medicine. But 'transform' is a decade-scale word, not a headline-scale one.
